frames.question: What does saving $200 a month at 5% become after 10 years?
frames.narration: If you save $200 a month at 5% interest, after 10 years you’ve put in $24,000 and earned about $7,056—so roughly $31,056 total. The chart shows both the “what you added” and the “interest earned” year by year; drag the monthly amount to see the what-if.

tour.say: First, look at the stacked flow: each year’s balance is split into what you deposited and the interest earned, so you can watch the gap widen with compounding.
Now the line chart makes the totals feel tangible—Year 10 lands around thirty-one thousand dollars, with the principal and interest shown as separate series.
Those headline numbers are the whole answer: after ten years you’d deposit twenty-four thousand, earn about seven thousand, and end up near thirty-one thousand.
And the donut shows the same result as a share: most is your deposits, and roughly a fifth to a quarter is interest earned.
If you want to reproduce it: monthly rate equals five percent divided by twelve, then we use the standard monthly-annuity future value formula.

frames.question: Why does compound interest beat simple interest? It's on my econ exam.
frames.narration: Compound interest beats simple because the interest you earn gets added back into the balance, so future interest is calculated on a bigger and bigger base. Simple interest keeps paying interest only on the original principal, so growth stays linear instead of exponential-ish.

spec.title: Compound vs Simple Interest
spec.sub: Compounding reinvests interest, so the base grows and future interest grows too.
spec.opener: Compound interest beats simple because the interest you earn gets added back into the balance, so future interest is calculated on a bigger and bigger base. Simple interest keeps paying interest only on the original principal, so growth stays linear instead of exponential-ish.

props.title: Compound interest grows faster
props.summary: Each period’s interest becomes part of the new principal, so the interest base increases over time.

blocks.note: Compound interest updates the balance each period; your interest then earns interest next period, which is the whole growth advantage.

props.title: Why compounding “feeds back” every period
props.caption: Think of each period’s interest as a new load that increases the next period’s starting point—so later “moment” is larger.

blocks.note: This diagram is an intuition pump: every time you add interest back in, you raise the next step’s starting point, so effects accumulate more.

props.title: Same rate, compounding vs simple over time
props.footer: Compounding is the faster-growing curve because the base increases each period.

blocks.note: This conceptual chart shows the pattern: simple grows by a fixed increment, while compounding climbs faster as the base keeps increasing.
Simple uses principal only (P·r·t), while compound raises (1 + r/n) to a power, reflecting repeated reinvestment.

props.title: Compounding: interest rate on a growing base
props.caption: As time goes on, the “effective principal” rises, so the next period’s interest is larger even with the same r.

blocks.note: A good way to picture it: compounding increases the balance, so applying the same interest rate later yields a bigger interest amount.

events.title: Principal exists
events.detail: Your balance entering the period is the base.

events.title: Interest is calculated
events.detail: You compute interest as a % of the current balance.

events.title: Interest is added back
events.detail: Now the next period starts with principal plus last period’s interest.

events.title: Repeat the feedback loop
events.detail: Because the base is larger, future interest gets bigger each time.

blocks.note: That end-of-period “add interest to the balance” step is the feedback loop that makes compound interest win.

options.name: Compound interest
options.sub: Same r each period, but bigger interest $ later

props.recommendation: If the rate is positive and time is › 1 period, compounding almost always produces a larger final amount than simple interest.

blocks.note: For econ exams: emphasize the base—simple pays on P, compounding pays on P plus all prior interest.

props.title: How to answer in one exam paragraph
items: Start with the principal: simple interest keeps using the original P as the base.
Then state the feedback: compound adds interest to the balance each period.
Conclude with growth: because the base increases, interest amounts rise over time.
Mention compounding frequency: more frequent compounding means more “reinvestment” opportunities.

blocks.note: Use this structure: base stays fixed in simple, but in compound the base increases, so growth accelerates.
